findings.title: refreshHistory leaves stale file copies in toolUseResult and turns partial reads into whole files
findings.summary: For each refreshed Read, build.mjs replaces only the tool_result text. Line 7 of both follow-up histories still holds the old output-format.md in toolUseResult.file.content (lines 61 and 64 differ). A Read with offset or limit would be replaced by the whole file. A Read of a file that no longer exists stays stale with no warning. In today's resumed eval run, the stale copy did not reach the model.

claims.claim: Only the tool_result text is replaced; the same event's toolUseResult.file keeps the recorded copy, so the fixtures hold two versions of output-format.md.
claims.evidence: build.mjs:139-143 assigns only part.content. In the follow-up histories, the output-format.md tool_result matches the current file, but toolUseResult.file.content differs at lines 61 and 64. Line 61 lacks 'including ★ recommendations they accepted with `ok` or by skipping a question'. Line 64 lacks 'Answers the user accepted are not assumptions, so don't repeat them there.' This is at line 7 of both files. The copies in save-to-file, and of the other references, are current.

claims.claim: When the stale copy entered.
claims.evidence: At 998e0c8 ('fresh histories') and at HEAD, the tool_result has the new wording and toolUseResult has the old. output-format.md has had the new wording since 124b72b.

claims.claim: A Read with offset/limit is replaced by the whole file, numbered from 1.
claims.evidence: Latent. A fixture Read {offset: 4, limit: 2} of questions.md was refreshed to the whole file, through '88\t'. No committed Read has offset or limit: every input has only file_path.

claims.claim: The refreshed text gains an extra final 'N\t' line.
claims.evidence: That final numbered empty line is Claude Code's own format for whole-file reads. In today's live 2.1.317 trace, each of the four Read results equals build.mjs's numbering of the current file, ending '108\t', '88\t', '104\t' and '59\t'.

claims.claim: A Read of a file that no longer exists is left stale, with no warning.
claims.evidence: Latent. A fixture Read of /plugin/skills/prompt-engine/references/gone.md kept '1\told' and printed nothing. The guard at build.mjs:143 is 'numbered !== undefined'.

claims.claim: Claude Code reads toolUseResult.file.content from transcript entries (the reviewer couldn't confirm how resume uses it).
claims.evidence: Checked in 2.1.317. Code whose log lines name it 'extractReadFilesFromMessages' sets 'ye=J?.file?.content' and uses 'ye.trim()' when the message has one tool_result; otherwise it strips the numbers from the tool_result text. It stores the result with 'contentFromTranscript:!0'. That cache backs Edit/Write checks such as 'File has been modified since read, either by the user or by a linter.' It is not sent to the model.

claims.claim: The stale copy changes what the model sees.
claims.evidence: I checked today's resumed run. evals/followup-ok-accepts-recommendations/00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001.jsonl was written by that run and is gitignored (.gitignore:9). The stale wording appears only in row 10 (the stored toolUseResult) and in 0 API request rows. The tool results sent (row 31) carry 'including ★ recommendations they accepted'. No file-change attachment was added. /plugin does not exist on this Mac. This is one run, so it shows what happened, not every code path.

claims.claim: (Extra) A failed Read is overwritten.
claims.evidence: Latent. A fixture tool_result with is_error: true and 'File does not exist.', for a file that exists now, became '1\t# Asking clarifying questions...' while keeping is_error: true ($W/fixes/is-error.mjs).

findings.reproduction:
$W = <scratch>/work/verify-scripts-build.
- `node $W/fixes/compare20.mjs . evals/followup-ok-accepts-recommendations/history.jsonl evals/followup-partial-answers/history.jsonl evals/save-to-file/history.jsonl`, run read-only on the real repo. For output-format.md in both follow-up histories: 'tool_result == current numbered: true | toolUseResult.file.content == current: false | differing lines: [61,64] | numLines=108 totalLines=108 startLine=1'. Every other Read: true. The two follow-up histories are byte-identical (cmp).
- grep -n gives line 7 in both files.
- Recorded line 61: '- **[your answer]** — something from their answers to your questions;'. Current line 61: '... to your questions, including ★ recommendations they accepted with `ok` or by skipping a question;'.
- Format of a whole-file Read: toolUseResult.file.content === the file text, numLines = totalLines = split('\n').length, startLine = 1. This holds in the committed fixtures and in /private/tmp/e-7HBxcP/out/trace.jsonl.
- Latent paths, current build, from $W/fixes/test-candidate.mjs and $W/fixes/is-error.mjs: 'partial read ... current build turns it into the whole file: true'; 'missing file: current build leaves it silently: true'; the failed Read became '1\t# Asking clarifying questions...' with is_error: true.
- Binary: `grep -a -b -o 'toolUseResult[^;]\{0,160\}file[?]\{0,1\}\.content'` found one offset, and dd around it showed the code in the claims. A grep for contentFromTranscript showed its consumers.
findings.refutation: I tried to show the stale copy is harmless, and for the model's input it was, as far as I could see: no API request row contains it. The cache it seeds is keyed to /plugin/..., which does not exist where evals run, and today's resumed run added no attachment from it. That lowers the severity. It doesn't remove the defect: the fixture holds two versions, and the missing-file path is as silent as finding 15. For example, renaming a reference file would leave follow-up evals reading the old text while every check passes. I checked whether it was fixed after 34d9caa: build.mjs and evals/ are unchanged. The partial-read and failed-Read paths are latent; no committed recording has either.

audit.reasoning: Line 7 of both follow-up fixtures holds two versions of output-format.md. The tool_result matches the current file. toolUseResult.file.content is the text recorded at 8a15447 and differs at lines 61 and 64. The two copies split at 998e0c8, the commit that added refreshHistory, because build.mjs:139-143 updates only the tool_result. build.mjs is unchanged since then. On resume, Claude Code 2.1.317 loads that field into its read-file cache (contentFromTranscript), not into the prompt. In today's resumed run, the old wording reached no API request. The other paths are latent but behave as the finding says: a Read with offset/limit is replaced by the whole file, a Read of a deleted file stays stale with no warning, and a failed Read is overwritten. Confirmed, minor.
audit.checks_run: compare20-audit.mjs, read-only on the repo: in both follow-up histories, line 7 (output-format.md) has tool_result equal to the current numbered file and file.content differing at lines [61,64]. Every other Read, including all of save-to-file, is current. Every Read input has only file_path. git show at three commits: 8a15447 has the old wording in both copies; 998e0c8 and HEAD have the new wording in the tool_result and the old in toolUseResult. Latent paths, current build.mjs: a Read with offset 4 and limit 2 became the whole 88-line file and toolUseResult stayed 'OLD'; a Read of gone.md was left unchanged with no error; an is_error result became '1\t# Asking clarifying questions…' and kept is_error: true. 2.1.317 binary (extractReadFilesFromMessages): it reads 'ye=J?.file?.content', uses ye.trim() when the message holds one tool_result, and stores it with 'contentFromTranscript:!0'. Resumed transcript evals/followup-ok-accepts-recommendations/00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001.jsonl, gitignored by .gitignore:9-10: the old wording is only on line 11 (the copied toolUseResult); the api-request-blob on line 32 has only the new wording; there is no edited_text_file attachment. /plugin doesn't exist on this Mac. Live trace /private/tmp/e-7HBxcP/out/trace.jsonl: the whole-file Reads end '108\t', '88\t', '104\t' and '59\t' and equal build.mjs's numbering; tool_use_result.file has content equal to the file, numLines = totalLines = split length, and startLine 1. Candidate in a copy with fix B: only toolUseResult.file.content changes on line 7 of each follow-up history, with key order kept; save-to-file is unchanged; checks are clean; 32/32 tests pass.
audit.evidence_errors: Two small errors. (1) The row numbers in the resumed transcript are off by one: the stale wording is on line 11 and the API request blob on line 32 (counting from 1), where the verifier says rows 10 and 31. (2) In /private/tmp/e-7HBxcP/out/trace.jsonl the field is named tool_use_result (stream-json), not toolUseResult. Its values match what the verifier says.
audit.fix_corrections: None needed. I re-verified the candidate as described above.

findings.fix_assessment: Updating toolUseResult.file is right, and for whole-file reads I verified the exact shape Claude Code writes, so it can be matched. Throwing on a missing file is right, but it must skip is_error results; otherwise a recording with a legitimately failed Read would never build. The reviewer's slicing for offset/limit depends on Claude Code's partial-read format, both the tool_result numbering and the toolUseResult fields. I couldn't verify that format without a billed run, and no recording has a partial read, so throwing ('re-record') is simpler and safe. I tested this candidate together with the finding 15 change. After one build, the only change to the committed files is line 7 of each follow-up history (toolUseResult.file.content); save-to-file is unchanged. --check is clean, validate is OK, and all 32 root tests pass with the finding 13 fix.
findings.proposed_fix:
In refreshHistory (scripts/build.mjs:136-143):
1. For each Read id, store {rel, partial}, where partial is true when input.offset or input.limit is present.
2. Skip tool_results with is_error: true.
3. For a partial read, throw 'history.jsonl reads part of <rel> (offset/limit); re-record it'.
4. When readPluginFile returns undefined, throw 'history.jsonl reads <rel>, which no longer exists; re-record it'.
5. After refreshing the tool_result, if row.toolUseResult?.file?.filePath === '/plugin/' + rel, set file.content to the current text, numLines and totalLines to current.split('\n').length, and startLine to 1.
Then run node scripts/build.mjs: it rewrites line 7 of the two follow-up histories and nothing else. Add tests: toolUseResult is refreshed; a partial read throws; a missing file throws; a failed Read is left as it was. A combined, tested version is at $W/fixes/candidate-refresh.mjs.
owner_questions: Low stakes: OK for build.mjs to refuse a recording whose Read used offset or limit, so it must be re-recorded (a billed call of up to $1)? The alternative is to refresh the same line window, as the reviewer proposed, but Claude Code's partial-read format isn't verified here. No current recording has a partial read.

Low stakes; the default is fine. Should build.mjs refuse a recording whose Read used offset or limit, so that it has to be re-recorded (a billed call capped at $1 by record-history.mjs)? No committed recording has a partial read.

findings.title: Impossible or future last_verified dates pass validation and turn off the monthly re-check; an unknown status crashes the validator
findings.summary: validate.mjs:201 checks last_verified only against /^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/. Impossible dates (2025-13-45, 2024-02-30) and future ones (2099-01-01) pass and are printed as 'last checked ...' in the generated reference. verify-data.yml's monthly check never lists the impossible or the future one. An unknown status, or a missing sources array, makes buildAll throw at validate.mjs:216. The validator then dies with a stack trace and drops the errors it had already found. All 12 entries today are dated 2026-10-29 and have valid statuses.

claims.claim: last_verified is checked only by a format regex.
claims.evidence: validate.mjs:201.

claims.claim: Impossible or future dates pass and are printed as 'last checked ...' in the generated reference that ships in every format.
claims.evidence: validate says OK. media-targets.md shows '(last checked 2025-13-45)', '(last checked 2099-01-01)' and '(last checked 2024-02-30)'. build also rewrote the knowledge file and content.ts.

claims.claim: verify-data.yml never flags such an entry: Date.parse gives NaN for the impossible date, and the future one is never 60 days old.
claims.evidence: I ran the workflow's script, copied verbatim from verify-data.yml:26-31, on that data: '1 stale entries', only 2024-02-30. On Node 24.21.0, Date.parse('2025-13-45') is NaN, Date.parse('2099-01-01') is 4070908800000, and 2024-02-30 rolls over to 2024-03-01. The workflow uses Node 22 (verify-data.yml:21), which I couldn't test here.

claims.claim: This defeats the 'facts may have changed since they were checked' reminder.
claims.evidence: That phrase isn't in the repo. The substance holds: the monthly re-check misses these entries.

claims.claim: An unknown status makes the validator die with a stack trace, without printing errors it already found such as 'needs https sources'.
claims.evidence: With status 'verifed' and an http:// source: exit 1 with 'Error: media-targets: unknown status "verifed" for midjourney' and a stack trace. Neither the 'bad status' error (validate.mjs:199) nor 'needs https sources' (:200) is printed. Exit 1 means it can't pass by mistake, and the thrown message names the entry.

claims.claim: New: a missing sources array also crashes, with a less helpful message.
claims.evidence: 'TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'join')' from build.mjs:47. It doesn't name the entry, and the error from validate.mjs:200 is lost.

findings.reproduction:
In a copy of HEAD, set last_verified to 2025-13-45 (midjourney), 2099-01-01 (gpt-image) and 2024-02-30 (gemini-image).
node scripts/build.mjs → wrote media-targets.md, the knowledge file and content.ts
node scripts/validate.mjs → 'validate: OK (...)'
grep → media-targets.md lines 7, 18 and 29 show '(last checked 2025-13-45)', '(last checked 2099-01-01)' and '(last checked 2024-02-30)'
verify-data.yml script, verbatim → '1 stale entries'; stale.md lists only 2024-02-30
Status 'verifed' + source http://example.com/docs → exit 1, 'Error: media-targets: unknown status "verifed" for midjourney'; 0 'bad status' or 'needs https sources' lines
sources deleted → exit 1, 'TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'join')'
With the reviewer's fix:
  bad dates → 'midjourney: last_verified must be a real YYYY-MM-DD date', 'gpt-image: last_verified 2099-01-01 is in the future', 'gemini-image: last_verified must be a real YYYY-MM-DD date'
  bad status → 'bad status "verifed"', 'needs https sources', 'build failed: media-targets: unknown status ...'
  no sources → 'needs https sources', 'build failed: Cannot read properties of undefined ...'
  clean copy → OK; 13/13 validate tests pass
findings.refutation: Today's data is valid: 12 entries, all dated 2026-10-29, all with valid statuses. Nothing wrong ships today. The crash still exits 1, so it can't cause a false pass; the problem is how errors are reported. The cited files are unchanged since 34d9caa. Minor, as the reviewer said.

audit.reasoning:
validate.mjs:201 only checks the date's format. I set midjourney, gpt-image and gemini-image to 2025-13-45, 2099-01-01 and 2024-02-30. validate says 'validate: OK', and media-targets.md:7, :18 and :29 print those dates as 'last checked'.

I ran the verify-data.yml script verbatim. It lists 1 stale entry, only 2024-02-30. On Node 24.21.0, Date.parse gives NaN for 2025-13-45, 4070908800000 for 2099-01-01, and turns 2024-02-30 into 2024-03-01. I didn't run the workflow's Node 22.

With status 'verifed' and an http source, validate exits 1 showing only the thrown 'unknown status' error and a stack trace. The 'bad status' and 'needs https sources' errors it had collected are never printed.

With sources deleted, the error is a TypeError from build.mjs:47 that doesn't name the entry.

All 12 entries today are dated 2026-10-29 and have valid statuses. Unchanged since 34d9caa.
audit.checks_run:
- Read validate.mjs:196-218, build.mjs:25-51 and verify-data.yml.
- Mutation copies: bad dates (build, validate, grep of media-targets.md, and the workflow script extracted verbatim), unknown status with an http source, and missing sources. Checked exit codes.
- Applied the proposed check and guard (tools/patch18-21.mjs) and re-ran each case.
- Probed the date check on 20 inputs, and the hardened workflow filter.
- Ran the documented chain (build --check, then validate) and `node scripts/build.mjs` on the broken-data copies with the guard applied.
- Grepped mcp/src for last_verified: only the ids are used.
audit.fix_corrections:
The date check works as proposed. I tested it on 20 inputs at 2026-11-03T14:06Z:
- Today and tomorrow pass.
- 2026-11-05, 2099-01-01 and 2028-02-29 are rejected as in the future.
- 2025-13-45, 2024-02-30, 2026-02-29, 2026-1-29, 20261029, undefined, null, a leading space, a full ISO time and a trailing newline are rejected as not real dates.
- 0000-01-01 and 1969-12-31 pass, but verify-data would list them as stale.
The guard works too, but on its own it isn't enough. Every documented chain runs build.mjs before validate: CONTRIBUTING.md:28, docs/publishing.md:40, .claude/CLAUDE.md:23 and ci.yml:21. CONTRIBUTING.md:75 tells contributors to run `node scripts/build.mjs` after editing the JSON. With the guard applied, both still die with the raw stack trace (tested), and the missing-sources message still names no entry.
Add two things:
- In renderMediaTargets, throw a named error when `!Array.isArray(t.sources)`, such as 'media-targets: midjourney needs a sources array'.
- In build.mjs main(), catch the error, print 'build failed: <message>' and exit 1 instead of showing the stack.
The hardened verify-data filter lists 2025-13-45, 2024-02-30 and a missing date (tested).

findings.fix_assessment:
Correct (tested). On 14 inputs (UTC time was 2026-11-03T10:45):
- Accepted: 2026-10-29, today (2026-11-03) and tomorrow (2026-11-04). The one day of slack covers time zones.
- Rejected as future: 2026-11-05, 2099-01-01, and 2028-02-29, a real date that is still in the future.
- Rejected as not a real date: 2025-13-45, 2024-02-30, 2026-02-29, 2026-1-29, 20261029, undefined and ' 2026-10-29'.

The guard turns all three crash cases into listed errors. The validator only depends on the clock for the future check, which can't start failing later for a date that passes today.

Optional: harden verify-data.yml as well, so an impossible (NaN) date is listed. Tested: the hardened filter lists 2025-13-45 and 2024-02-30.

findings.title: The universal prompt's behavior test passes outputs that break the contract, and its runs depend on the developer's own config
findings.summary: Three of the universal test's checks can't fail on the breaks they are named for: a missing reply line, a menu with no options, and a full prompt under a bold label all pass. The runs pass only --system-prompt and --tools ''. Claude Code's CLI reference says --tools "doesn't affect MCP tools", and claude.ai connectors load in --print mode, so a run on this Mac would likely see MCP tools. The reviewer's replacement menu regex would wrongly fail the correct "Done ★" menu for image prompts.

claims.claim: 'ok reply line' is /\bok\b/i, so any "OK" passes without the reply line
claims.evidence: universal-test.mjs:47. Synthetic S1 has no reply line and ends "It is OK to skip any question." All 4 QUESTIONS checks pass.

claims.claim: 'what next menu' looks only for "What next?"
claims.evidence: universal-test.mjs:42. Synthetic S3, a full output ending "### What next?\nLet me know.", passes all 7 STRUCTURE checks.

claims.claim: 'no full prompt yet' misses a full prompt under a bold label
claims.evidence: universal-test.mjs:48. Synthetic S2, with "**Full prompt**" and a code block after the questions, passes.

claims.claim: The runs pass only --system-prompt and --tools ''
claims.evidence: universal-test.mjs:26-27. The other flags are --model, --output-format json, --max-budget-usd 0.5 and --resume, and none of them isolates the run.

claims.claim: --tools covers only "the built-in set"
claims.evidence: `claude --help` on 2.1.317 says: "Specify the list of available tools from the built-in set". The CLI reference, fetched today, says: "The flag doesn't affect MCP tools; to deny those too, use --disallowedTools "mcp__*"".

claims.claim: CLAUDE.md, hooks and MCP servers are turned off only by --bare, --safe-mode or --strict-mcp-config, none of which are passed
claims.evidence: None of them is passed. "Only" is overstated: --setting-sources, --restricted and --disallowedTools "mcp__*" also restrict parts of this.

claims.claim: So results vary with the developer's ~/.claude setup
claims.evidence: The runtime effect isn't checkable here without a billed run. On this Mac there is no ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and no hooks in ~/.claude/settings.json. There is one MCP server in ~/.claude.json, and this Claude Code session lists claude.ai connectors (Google Drive, Claude Docs, ResumeQuick and others). Changelog 2.1.83: "Fixed claude.ai MCP connectors ... not being available in single-turn --print mode". Separately, today's live U3 turn 3 (run with --strict-mcp-config) said "This session's working directory is a scratch folder, not a git repository". So Claude Code passes context that a chatbot wouldn't have (one run).

findings.reproduction:
- node <scratch>/work/verify-tests-coverage/checks.mjs <live/universal> (STRUCTURE and QUESTIONS copied verbatim from universal-test.mjs:34-49). S1: all 4 QUESTIONS checks PASS. S2: "PASS no full prompt yet". S3: 7 of 7 STRUCTURE checks PASS. Every current check also passes the live U1, U2, U3 turns 1-2, U5, U6 and U7.
- The reviewer's regexes on the same inputs fail S1, S2 and S3, as they should. They also fail live U2, wrongly: U2's "1) Done ★ (paste it into Midjourney, since I can't generate images)" follows output-format.md:77 and universal/prompt-engine.md:56.
- node <scratch>/work/verify-tests-coverage/checks-corrected.mjs <live/universal>: the corrected checks fail S1-S3, pass a synthetic "Done ★" menu, and pass every live output on the reply line, the no-full-prompt check and the menu.
- `claude --help` (2.1.317): --safe-mode "Start with all customizations (CLAUDE.md, skills, installed plugins, hooks, MCP servers, ...) disabled ... Auth, model selection, built-in tools and plugins, and permissions work normally". --bare: "Anthropic auth is strictly ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or apiKeyHelper ... (OAuth and keychain are never read)".
- Claude Code CHANGELOG.md, downloaded to <scratch>/work/verify-tests-coverage/dl-cc-changelog/: --safe-mode was added in 2.1.169, and --strict-mcp-config was already being fixed by 2.1.274. Both are older than the 2.1.312 pin.
- The 2.1.317 bundle builds the stream-json init event as {type:"system",subtype:"init",...,tools:...,mcp_servers:...}.
findings.refutation: I checked whether --system-prompt alone isolates the run. It doesn't: the CLI reference says it "Replace[s] the entire system prompt", and MCP tools and Claude Code's added context still apply, as U3 turn 3 suggests. I also checked whether the loose checks are harmless because the model always writes these strings. Today's outputs do contain "Reply `ok` to accept every ★" and full menus, so they pass for the right reason today. But the checks can't fail when the model breaks the rule, and today's runs do break the menu rule (Save to file offered with tools disabled), which no check sees. Severity stays minor: this is a dev script, run by hand and billed.

audit.reasoning:
Confirmed.
- Loose checks. I extracted universal-test.mjs:34-49 verbatim and ran it on new inputs. The current checks pass:
  - a question turn with no reply line, ending "Let me know if these look OK.";
  - question turns that hold a full prompt under "**Full prompt**", under a plain "Full prompt:" label, or as "Here is a draft:" followed by a fence;
  - final outputs whose menu is just "Let me know.", lacks Run it now, or puts the ★ on Refine.
- Flags. universal-test.mjs:26-27 passes only --system-prompt, --tools '', --model, --output-format json and --max-budget-usd, plus --resume on turn 2.
- What --tools covers. The CLI reference, fetched today, says --tools "doesn't affect MCP tools; to deny those too, use --disallowedTools "mcp__*"". It also says "" removes EndConversation "only when no MCP tools remain". claude --help on 2.1.317 says --tools picks "from the built-in set".
- This Mac. There is no ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and there are no hooks. There is one user MCP server (claude-design), plus claude.ai connectors. Changelog 2.1.83 says connectors load in single-turn --print mode. So the script as written would likely carry MCP tools here. I didn't run it, because it makes billed calls.
- Added context. Today's U3 turn 3 knew its folder "is a scratch folder, not a git repository", so Claude Code adds context even with --system-prompt (one run).
- Not fixed. universal-test.mjs is unchanged since 124b72b.
- Plan. plan.md:177 approved this exact command, but its stated purpose (tools disabled, like a chatbot) isn't met. That makes this a defect, not an owner choice.
- Related. Two of the loose regexes also appear in the eval graders (coding-vague-asks-questions/graders/04 and 05). Those belong to step 1b.

audit.evidence_errors: None material. Every quote, line number and changelog entry I re-checked matches. That MCP tools would load at runtime is still a likely effect, not an observed one.
audit.fix_corrections:
(1) 'no full prompt yet'. The corrected regex still passes a question turn with a plain "Full prompt:" label, or with a draft in a fence (tested). Add a fence test: (t) => !/```|(#+\s*|\*\*)Full prompt|\|\s*Clear goal\s*\||What next\?/i.test(t). U3 turn 1 and U7 contain no fences and still pass.
(2) 'what next menu'. The corrected regex passes a menu with no ★ if a later sentence contains "done ★" (contrived, but tested). Anchor the label to a numbered option: /What next\?[\s\S]*?\d[.)]\s*\**(Run it now|Fill placeholders|Try it here|Done)\**\s*★[\s\S]*Refine/i. This passes U1, U2, U3 turn 2, U5, U6, and Done and Fill-placeholders menus.
(3) Save to file: use the list-option form given under finding 5.
(4) Keep 'ok reply line' strict. It is the contract string (replyLine in data/contract.json). It fails Reply "ok" written with quotes, which does deviate from that string.
(5) Isolation. Add --disallowedTools "mcp__*" alongside --safe-mode and --strict-mcp-config; the CLI reference names it for exactly this purpose. findings.title: Re-running a release fails before npm and the MCP Registry, so a failed publish can't be finished from CI
findings.summary: release.yml checks nothing before `gh release create` or `mcp-publisher publish`. Both refuse to publish the same tag or version twice, and GitHub re-runs a job from its first step. So once the GitHub release exists, every re-run fails at that step and can't reach npm or the registry. Nothing is lost: npm and the registry can still be published by hand (docs/publishing.md:20, :64).

claims.claim: Only the npm step checks whether its target already has this version.
claims.evidence: release.yml:44-48 is the only guard (npm view). The GitHub release step (:30-38) has none. The registry step (:54-69) waits for npm (:58-66) but never asks the registry. git log --follow shows one commit, 7fb1b1a, so the file is unchanged since 34d9caa.

All have `return fmt.Errorf("a release with the same tag name already exists: %s", opts.TagName)`. The check is a HEAD request to releases/tags/{tag} (http.go v2.89.0:144-166).

findings.refutation: Fixed after 34d9caa? No: the file has a single commit, 7fb1b1a. Does gh skip or overwrite an existing release? No: every version I read errors out (v2.89.0, v2.103.2 on the runner, v2.103.3 latest). Can a re-run start at a later step? No: GitHub re-runs whole jobs, and release.yml has one job and no workflow_dispatch. Is it a dead end? No. npm by hand (publishing.md:20) and the registry by hand (publishing.md:64) can finish a failed release. Deleting the GitHub release and re-running would also work, but that isn't documented. Nothing irreversible happens, so I rate this minor rather than major. A failure inside the release step itself doesn't block re-runs, because gh deletes its draft (create.go v2.89.0:533-541). The detail that a re-run after full success 'fails at the registry step' is off: it fails earlier, at the GitHub release step.

audit.reasoning: The defect is real at HEAD. release.yml is byte-identical to 34d9caa, and its only commit is 7fb1b1a. Only the npm step checks its target first (.github/pending-workflows/release.yml:45-48). The GitHub release step (:30-38) runs `gh release create` with assets. gh then refuses with 'a release with the same tag name already exists' (create.go:499-506 at v2.89.0, :503-511 at v2.103.2 and at v2.103.3). v2.103.2 is the gh on ubuntu-latest (runner-images Ubuntu2404-Readme.md:112). The registry rejects a duplicate version (registry_service.go:279-280 at v1.8.6, :301-302 at v1.8.7). mcp-publisher turns any non-2xx reply into an error (publish.go:149) and exits 1 (main.go:65). GitHub re-runs whole jobs, never single steps (github/docs re-run-workflows-and-jobs.md:4), and release.yml has one job. So once the GitHub release exists, every re-run stops at that step. One detail in the finding is wrong, as the verifier says: a re-run after a full success fails at the GitHub release step, not at the registry step. Nothing is lost. npm and the registry can be finished by hand (docs/publishing.md:20, :64). Deleting the GitHub release and re-running also works today, because immutable releases are off for this repo (API: enabled false). That route would close if immutable releases were turned on: a deleted immutable release's tag name can't be reused (immutable-releases.md:22). The verifier missed one thing that makes this failure more likely. `npm publish` runs prepublishOnly (mcp/package.json:48), so the whole MCP suite runs a second time after the GitHub release exists. findings.title: The only CI path to npm (NPM_TOKEN) is scheduled to stop working in January 2027, and the trusted-publishing alternative needs a newer npm than Node 22 bundles
findings.summary: release.yml's only CI path to npm is the NPM_TOKEN secret, on Node 22, which bundles npm 10.9.x. npm's docs, checked today, say three things that publishing.md:19-22 leaves out: direct publishing with granular tokens ends in January 2027; a CI token needs Bypass 2FA, which is off by default; and trusted publishing needs npm 11.5.1 or later plus a package that already exists. Nothing user-facing breaks. Publishing by hand still works.

claims.claim: The npm step publishes with NODE_AUTH_TOKEN from the NPM_TOKEN secret. It is the only CI path to npm.
claims.evidence: release.yml:42 `NODE_AUTH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}`. :49-52 skip when it's empty. :53 `npm publish --provenance --access public`. The file is byte-identical at 34d9caa and HEAD.

claims.claim: publishing.md:21 recommends that setup.
claims.evidence: It is the second of three options (:20 publish by hand, :21 token, :22 trusted publishing). It isn't recommended over the others. publishing.md:12 and :93 do name NPM_TOKEN as what CI needs.

claims.claim: npm will remove direct publishing with granular access tokens in January 2027.
claims.evidence: about-access-tokens.mdx:82 at npm/documentation 92817e7 (file last changed 2026-09-10): "will be removed in **January 2027**". The same text is on the live docs.npmjs.com page today. It's npm's stated plan, and the date could move.

claims.claim: npm's recommended replacement is trusted publishing.
claims.evidence: The deprecation paragraph itself (:82) names "Read and write (stage only)" tokens with maintainer approval as the migration. Trusted publishing is recommended separately: :94 and the 2FA page ("For CI/CD workflows, consider using trusted publishing").

claims.claim: Trusted publishing needs npm CLI 11.5.1 or later and Node 22.14.0 or later.
claims.evidence: trusted-publishers.mdx:9; the live page says the same.

claims.claim: `node-version: 22` installs npm 10.9.x.
claims.evidence: nodejs.org/dist/index.json today: every v22 release bundles npm 10.x (latest v22.23.4 bundles 10.9.9). The first release with npm 11.5.1 or later is v24.5.0, and v24.22.2 bundles 11.19.1. npm v10.9.9 has no lib/utils/oidc.js (404); v11.5.1 has it.

claims.claim: publishing.md:22's 'small changes' leave out the newer npm that trusted publishing needs.
claims.evidence: :22 says only "release.yml would need small changes". What's actually needed: Node 24, dropping the empty-token skip (:49-52, which would skip every OIDC publish when no secret is set), the workflow in .github/workflows/ (trusted-publishers.mdx:50; it is parked in .github/pending-workflows/), and a trusted publisher with `npm publish` allowed.

claims.claim: publishing.md:21 doesn't say which token options CI needs. Bypass 2FA is off by default, and when it's off, account and package 2FA settings apply.
claims.evidence: about-access-tokens.mdx:45 "set to false by default". creating-and-viewing-access-tokens.mdx:25-27. The 2FA page: "All packages now require two-factor authentication (2FA) or a granular access tokens with bypass 2FA enabled for creating and publishing packages." So a token made with the defaults can't publish from CI. I couldn't check the actual CI failure here: there's no npm account and no publish.

claims.claim: A new trusted-publisher configuration must complete its first publish within 2 days.
claims.evidence: trusted-publishers.mdx:232-234 says it "expires" otherwise. This rule appears only in the page's 'Multiple trusted publishers' view. The 'Single trusted publisher' view doesn't mention it.

claims.claim: Provenance is automatic with trusted publishing.
claims.evidence: trusted-publishers.mdx:266. npm v11.19.1 lib/utils/oidc.js:145-161 turns provenance on for public GitHub repos.

claims.claim: Trusted publishers are set up on the package's settings page, so the first publish has to be done by hand.
claims.evidence: trusted-publishers.mdx:37. npm-trust.mdx:34: "Package must exist: The package you're configuring must already exist on the npm registry." `npm view prompt-engine-mcp` returns E404 today. This settles the open question in publishing.md:22 and plan.md:184.

Fixed after 34d9caa? No. release.yml is identical, and publishing.md changed only at :81 and :87.
Is the January 2027 text stale? No. It's on the live page today and hasn't changed since 2026-09-10.
Could Node 22 do trusted publishing anyway? No. No Node 22 release bundles npm 11, and npm 10.9.9 has no OIDC code.
Does plan.md settle it? No. :184 records the 'manual or NPM_TOKEN' choice and flags first-publish trusted publishing as unverified. It makes no decision to keep tokens.

audit.evidence_errors:
1. The claim "npm's recommended replacement is trusted publishing" holds in full, not just in part. npm's CI/CD page says "we recommend using trusted publishing instead of access tokens" (using-private-packages-in-a-ci-cd-workflow.mdx:9-11). npm's CLI docs add that best practice is stage-only trust relationships (npm-stage.mdx:100-104).
2. "The first publish has to be done by hand" overstates it. Trusted publishing can't do the first publish, but a token can. A bypass token works until January 2027. So does `npm stage publish`, which npm says "will allow you to create a new package if it does not exist" (npm-stage.mdx:42; staged-publishing.mdx:9 says it creates a public 0.0.0-stage placeholder); you then approve it with 2FA. audit.fix_corrections:
1. Tell the owner that option (a) goes against npm's stated best practice. npm-stage.mdx:100-104 says to delete bypass tokens, to disallow tokens at the package level, and to allow only `npm stage publish` on trust relationships. Option (a) is still a fair choice if you want full automation.
2. Option (b) needs npm 11.15.0 or later (staged-publishing.mdx:13). Keep `node-version: 24` floating, so it resolves to v24.22.2 with npm 11.19.1. Don't pin an early 24.x: v24.0.0 through v24.17.x bundle older npm, and v24.0.0 through v24.4.1 are even below 11.5.1.
3. If the trusted publisher is created from the CLI instead of the website, `npm trust github` needs npm 11.15.0 or later, 2FA on the account, and `--allow-publish` (npm-trust.mdx:30-34 and :48-53).

The rest of the verifier's fix checks out: Node 24, keep the `npm view` skip, drop :41-42 and :49-52, tick `npm publish`, create the configuration no more than 2 days before the first tag whose version isn't on npm yet, and update the docs at :3, :12, :19-22, :62 and :93.

findings.fix_assessment:
The reviewer's direction is right: trusted publishing on Node 24, keep the `npm view` skip, drop the token and the empty-token skip. These parts check out: Node 24.22.2 bundles npm 11.19.1, setup-node v7 exists, and the skip check works on npm 11. Removing the empty-token branch is required, not optional: otherwise every OIDC publish is skipped when no secret is set. `--provenance` becomes optional.

The reviewer's fix has three gaps:
(1) It leaves out Allowed actions. Configurations created after 2026-09-03 allow only `npm stage publish` by default (trusted-publishers.mdx:92; `npm trust` requires `--allow-publish`). Unless `npm publish` is ticked, npm refuses the CI publish.
(2) The 2-day order is wrong. If 0.1.0 is published by hand and v0.1.0 is pushed, CI skips npm. Nothing then validates the new configuration, and it expires. Create it no more than 2 days before the first tag whose version isn't on npm yet.
(3) The open question in publishing.md:22 and plan.md:184 can now be answered (the package must exist first), and publishing.md:3's check date needs updating.

owner_questions:
How should CI publish to npm?
(a) Trusted publishing with direct `npm publish`. Fully automatic; this is my recommendation.
(b) `npm stage publish`, approving each version with 2FA on npmjs.com. Safer, but the registry job would skip until you approve, so you'd run the registry publish by hand.
(c) Publish by hand every release and remove npm from the workflow.
Also, may I update plan.md:184? It still says first-publish trusted publishing is unverified, but npm's docs now say the package must exist first.

How should CI publish to npm?
(a) Trusted publishing with direct `npm publish`. It's fully automatic, but npm's own best-practice list says to allow only staging.
(b) Trusted publishing with `npm stage publish` only. You approve each version on npmjs.com with 2FA, then run the MCP Registry publish by hand.
(c) Publish by hand at every release, and remove npm from the workflow.
Also, may plan.md:184 be updated? npm's docs say a package must exist before you can add a trusted publisher, so the first publish can't use trusted publishing.

findings.area: GitHub workflows (.github/pending-workflows: ci, release, evals, verify-data)
findings.title: Every step of the single release job gets contents: write and id-token: write, including third-party code
findings.summary: release.yml grants `contents: write` and `id-token: write` at the workflow level to its only job. That job also runs everything else: npm ci (postinstall scripts in @modelcontextprotocol/inspector 2.13.0 and esbuild 0.28.2), the build and tests, release.mjs, npm publish (whose prepublishOnly re-runs build and tests with NODE_AUTH_TOKEN set) and a downloaded mcp-publisher binary. Checkout persists the write token by default. The repo's `main` is unprotected, so compromised code in this job could push to the branch users install the plugin from.

claims.claim: Permissions are set at the workflow level, and everything runs in one job.
claims.evidence: release.yml:9-11 (`contents: write`, `id-token: write`). :13-14 define a single job, `release`. The file is identical at 34d9caa.

claims.claim: npm ci runs install scripts for inspector 2.13.0 and esbuild 0.28.2 (and fsevents).
claims.evidence: package-lock.json marks hasInstallScript at :848 (inspector) and :2756 (esbuild). npm view shows inspector `postinstall: node scripts/install-clients.mjs` and esbuild `postinstall: node install.js`. fsevents (:2944) is optional and macOS-only, so it doesn't install on ubuntu-latest.

claims.claim: The same job runs the TypeScript/vitest suite, the esbuild bundler and release.mjs.
claims.evidence: release.yml:22-29. release.mjs:51 runs `npm run pack:mcpb`, which runs bundle.mjs (esbuild) and pack-mcpb.mjs (the mcpb CLI).

claims.claim: npm publish's prepublishOnly (mcp/package.json:47) re-runs build and test with NODE_AUTH_TOKEN in the environment.
claims.evidence: The line is :48, not :47, and was :48 at 34d9caa too. release.yml:40-42 sets the token for a directory publish. npm v11.19.1 publish.js:99-107 runs prepublishOnly for directory publishes.

claims.claim: A downloaded binary runs in the same job.
claims.evidence: release.yml:67-69: `curl ... | tar xz mcp-publisher`, then `./mcp-publisher login github-oidc` and `publish`. That it isn't verified is finding 28.

claims.claim: actions/checkout keeps the write-scoped GITHUB_TOKEN available to later steps by default.
claims.evidence: checkout v7 (v7.0.1) README:33: "The auth token is persisted in the local git config ... Set `persist-credentials: false` to opt-out." action.yml: default true. README:16: since v6 the token sits in a file under $RUNNER_TEMP that git still uses. Documented; I didn't run it on GitHub.

claims.claim: Any step can request an OIDC token.
claims.evidence: GitHub docs oidc.md:595-608: the token is available through the ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL and ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN environment variables on the runner. npm's own oidc.js:64-65 reads them from process.env inside a run step. Documented; I didn't run it on GitHub.

claims.claim: A github-oidc login gives publish rights over every server under io.github.vipul-goel/*.
claims.evidence: Registry v1.8.6 github_oidc.go:291-294: `ResourcePattern: fmt.Sprintf("io.github.%s/*", claims.RepositoryOwner)`. The file is identical at v1.8.7 and main, and its comment says this is deliberate. The registry lists no io.github.vipul-goel servers today, so for now the extra reach covers only servers you publish later.

claims.claim: The registry docs warn that such a token can publish and overwrite any server in the namespace.

Fixed after 34d9caa? No; release.yml is identical.
Vendor practice: npm's trusted-publishing example (trusted-publishers.mdx:100-129) and the registry's example (github-actions.mdx:21-91) both run npm ci, tests and publish in one job with `id-token: write`. So that part is common practice. But both use `contents: read`. The excess here is `contents: write` for every step, the persisted token, and a long-lived NPM_TOKEN in the same job.
Likelihood: the lockfile pins exact versions with integrity hashes, and the actions are first-party. Exploiting this needs a malicious version already in the lockfile or a compromised action. That limits likelihood, not impact.
Impact: the repo is public, `main` is unprotected and has no rulesets, and publishing.md:9-10 says the plugin and `npx skills add` are served from `main`.
The workflow is parked, so nothing is exposed today. It goes live in step 2.
I keep the severity at major because of the unprotected `main`, but the likelihood is low.

audit.reasoning:
The core defect is real on this branch. release.yml (unchanged since 7fb1b1a) sets `contents: write` and `id-token: write` at the workflow level (:9-11), and it has a single job (:13-14). That job runs:
- npm ci (:25). The lockfile has install scripts for @modelcontextprotocol/inspector 2.13.0 (package-lock.json:848) and esbuild 0.28.2 (:2756). fsevents (:2944) is macOS-only, so it doesn't install on ubuntu-latest.
- tsc and vitest.
- release.mjs, which runs pack:mcpb (release.mjs:51).
- npm publish, whose prepublishOnly hook re-runs build and test while NODE_AUTH_TOKEN is set (mcp/package.json:48).
- An unverified mcp-publisher download (:67-69).

actions/checkout@v7 keeps the token for later steps by default (action.yml:54; README:33). Only `gh release create` (:36) needs `contents: write`. GitHub's own guidance is to raise permissions job by job (secure-use.md:34).

Repository settings today: main is unprotected and has 0 rulesets. So a stolen write token could push to the branch that users install the plugin from (publishing.md:9-10). The MCP Registry grants publish rights to io.github.<owner>/* (github_oidc.go:288-294; the same on main, and its comment says this is deliberate). The namespace has 0 servers today.

Not wrong. npm's example (trusted-publishers.mdx:100-129) and the registry's example (github-actions.mdx:21-91) do run npm ci and publish in one job with `id-token: write`, so that part is common practice. But both use `contents: read`.
Not already fixed: the file is identical at 34d9caa and HEAD.
Not an owner decision: the extra privilege is a plain least-privilege defect. Only the shape of the fix is a choice.

The likelihood is low:
- Only a v* tag push triggers the workflow, and vipul-goel is the only collaborator.
- The lockfile pins integrity hashes.
- The inspector's postinstall exits early under node_modules (install-clients.mjs:66-69), so npm ci fetches nothing unpinned.
- Nothing is live today: origin/main holds only README.md.
So the "major" rating rests on impact, not likelihood.

audit.fix_corrections:
1. If finding 32's `ci: uses: ./.github/workflows/ci.yml` job is merged into this split, give that job `permissions: contents: read`. With `permissions: {}` at the top, a called workflow can only keep or lower the caller's token permissions (reusing-workflow-configurations.md:91). ci.yml:8-9 asks for `contents: read`, so without this the call would be refused. This is a documented rule; I didn't run it on GitHub.
2. Prefer actions/download-artifact@v8 (v8.0.2, 2026-10-07). It is the current major, and it fails on a digest mismatch by default. Its release notes say earlier versions only logged a warning. v7 still works.
3. Not checkable here: how the split behaves on re-runs. Does "Re-run failed jobs" reuse the build artifact? Does "Re-run all jobs" clash on the artifact name? Test this when applying finding 25's guards, or set `overwrite: true` on the upload.

The rest of the verifier's fix holds:
- npm pack output has LICENSE and leaves out worker.js.
- A tarball publish runs no scripts.
- GH_REPO is needed when there's no checkout.
- The npm skip must stay.

findings.fix_assessment:
The reviewer's job split is the right fix. Only a separate job isolates credentials: scoping a secret to one step or setting `persist-credentials: false` doesn't, because steps in one job can read secrets from the Runner Worker's memory.

I checked its pieces:
- `npm pack` output contains LICENSE, and dist/worker.js is excluded (verified in a copy).
- Publishing a tarball runs no lifecycle scripts anyway, so `--ignore-scripts` is a harmless extra safeguard.
- bundle.mjs and pack-mcpb.mjs write outside mcp/dist, so packing after release.mjs is safe.
- `gh release create` without a checkout needs GH_REPO, and the reviewer included it.
- upload-artifact and download-artifact v7 accept the inputs used.

Gaps in the reviewer's version:
(1) Its npm job drops the `npm view` skip. A re-run, or the first release after a hand publish (publishing.md:20), would fail with "cannot publish over", and the registry job (needs: npm) would be skipped. Keep the skip, taking the version from `${GITHUB_REF_NAME#v}`.
(2) "The verified publisher" is vague. Verify the `.sigstore.json` that the v1.8.6 release ships; that is finding 28's fix.
(3) The npm job needs Node 24 for trusted publishing (finding 26).
(4) The registry job needs setup-node for its wait loop.
(5) An honest limit: a compromised build dependency can still tamper with the files it builds. The split stops credential theft and repository writes, not artifact tampering.

My draft at <scratch>/work/verify-workflows-release-b/r2/draft/release.yml parses, and its npm step passed a stub test. I haven't run it on GitHub, and actionlint isn't installed.
findings.proposed_fix:
In .github/pending-workflows/release.yml, put `permissions: {}` at the top and split the work into four jobs:
1. `build` (contents: read): checkout with `persist-credentials: false`; setup-node 22; in mcp/, npm ci, npm run build and npm test; then `node scripts/release.mjs --tag "$GITHUB_REF_NAME"`; then `npm pack --pack-destination ../dist` in mcp/; upload dist/ with actions/upload-artifact@v7 and `if-no-files-found: error`.
2. `github-release` (needs build; contents: write): download-artifact into dist/, then `gh release create` with `GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}` and `GH_REPO: ${{ github.repository }}`. No checkout.
3. `npm` (needs build; contents: read, id-token: write): setup-node 24 with registry-url; download-artifact; `version="${GITHUB_REF_NAME#v}"`; keep the `npm view` skip; then `npm publish "dist/prompt-engine-mcp-${version}.tgz" --access public --ignore-scripts`.
4. `registry` (needs npm; contents: read, id-token: write): checkout with `persist-credentials: false`; setup-node 22; `sigstore/cosign-installer@6f9f17788090df1f26f669e9d70d6ae9567deba6` (v4.1.2); the existing wait loop; download mcp-publisher v1.8.6 and its .sigstore.json and run `cosign verify-blob`; then login github-oidc and publish.

Update docs/publishing.md:24 to describe the per-job permissions, and :62 to describe the job order. Apply findings 25, 28 and 32 at the same time, since they edit the same file. Finding 32's `needs: ci` goes on `build`.
owner_questions:
Two choices.
(1) Do you want the full four-job split (recommended)? The lighter alternative is a separate GitHub-release job plus `persist-credentials: false` plus trusted publishing. That leaves `id-token: write` in the job that runs npm ci, as npm's and the registry's own examples do.
(2) `main` has no branch protection or rulesets. Do you want to protect it and limit who can push v* tags? Only you can change those settings.

findings.title: The mcp-publisher binary is downloaded and run without any checksum or signature check, contrary to the registry's own instructions
findings.summary: release.yml:67-69 downloads mcp-publisher v1.8.6 and runs it with no hash or signature check. The job holds `contents: write` and `id-token: write`. The registry's own GitHub Actions guide verifies a Sigstore bundle before extracting. The registry's releases aren't immutable, so pinning the tag doesn't pin the bytes. The asset is unchanged today.

claims.claim: The binary is downloaded and run with no checksum or signature check.
claims.evidence: release.yml:67 `curl -fsSL "https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/registry/releases/download/v1.8.6/mcp-publisher_linux_amd64.tar.gz" | tar xz mcp-publisher`; :68-69 run it. Unchanged since 7fb1b1a.

claims.claim: The job can mint OIDC tokens and holds a write-scoped GITHUB_TOKEN.
claims.evidence: release.yml:9-11 grant contents: write and id-token: write to the whole job. github/docs oidc.md:597-603 list ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL and ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN as variables 'on the runner'. actions/checkout v7 action.yml:52-54 sets persist-credentials to true by default, and README:33 says the token 'enables your scripts to run authenticated git commands'. main is unprotected: GET branches/main/protection returns 404 'Branch not protected', and rulesets is [].

claims.claim: Pinning v1.8.6 doesn't protect the asset, because release assets can be replaced.
claims.evidence: Every registry release from v1.8.0 to v1.8.7 reports "immutable": false. GitHub's immutable-releases doc (:22-23) says only immutable releases lock their tag and have assets that 'cannot be modified or deleted'.

The example at :64-83 uses sigstore/cosign-installer pinned by SHA (v4.1.2) and `cosign verify-blob`.

findings.refutation: Fixed after 34d9caa? No: release.yml is unchanged since 7fb1b1a. Do the v1.8.6 pin and HTTPS protect the bytes? No. HTTPS protects only the transfer, and the registry's releases aren't immutable, so anyone with write access to that repository can delete and re-upload an asset. Is the step unprivileged? No: the token is job-wide, checkout leaves it usable by later steps, and main is unprotected. Has the asset been tampered with? Not as of today: the file hash, checksums line 5, the API digest and the bundle digest all agree. I couldn't refute the finding. The likelihood is low, because it needs a compromise of the registry's releases. The impact is high: during a release, `contents: write` lets a swapped binary replace this repo's release assets, such as the .mcpb, or push to main. So I keep the severity at major. The manual path at publishing.md:64 has the same gap.

audit.reasoning: The defect is real at HEAD; release.yml is unchanged since 7fb1b1a. release.yml:67 pipes the v1.8.6 asset from curl straight into tar, and :68-69 run it. Nothing checks a hash or a signature. The whole job holds contents: write and id-token: write (:9-11). At the pinned tag, the registry's GitHub Actions guide says the examples 'verify its Sigstore bundle before extracting it' (docs/modelcontextprotocol-io/github-actions.mdx:14-17 at v1.8.6, identical at v1.8.7). That text arrived on 2026-10-24 (registry #1523), five days before release.yml was written (7fb1b1a, 2026-10-29). Every registry release from v1.7.8 to v1.8.7 reports immutable false, so pinning the tag doesn't pin the bytes. Nothing has been swapped so far. The asset I downloaded today hashes to 1fbe93fc...e21340, which matches line 5 of the checksums file, the API digest and the bundle's digest. One nuance: the registry's own quickstart still pipes curl into tar from releases/latest (quickstart.mdx:130 at v1.8.6). So 'contrary to the registry's own instructions' holds only for its CI guide, which is the one that applies here. The impact may be wider than the verifier says. Hosted runners have passwordless sudo (github/docs reference/runners/github-hosted-runners.md:77). The 2025 tj-actions/changed-files attack (CVE-2025-30066) read secrets out of the Runner.Worker process memory from a single step. So a swapped publisher could probably also reach NPM_TOKEN, which the npm step in the same job uses. I didn't test that. Major fits: low likelihood, high impact.

audit.fix_corrections: 1. The hash-pin fix works as written; I tested it, and the archive member really is named mcp-publisher. 2. The optional `persist-credentials: false` only goes part way. With passwordless sudo, a swapped binary can still read tokens and secrets from the runner's memory. The real containment is running the registry publish in its own job with only `id-token: write`, which is finding 27's fix. Do 27 and 28 together. 3. The manual check proposed for publishing.md:64 uses the checksums file from the same release. As the verifier says, that catches a broken download, not a swapped one. It's still worth adding.

findings.fix_assessment: Correct. I prefer the hash variant: it pins the exact bytes, needs no new third-party action, and cosign isn't in the ubuntu-24.04 image. A cosign check binds to the tag name refs/tags/v1.8.6, and the tag of a non-immutable release can move. Small improvements: keep the version and the hash next to each other in env, and extract into $RUNNER_TEMP instead of the checkout. mcp-publisher's token lives in ~/.config/mcp-publisher (login.go:30-35), so the binary's location doesn't matter. findings.proposed_fix:
In the 'Publish to the MCP Registry' step of .github/pending-workflows/release.yml, add
  env:
    MCP_PUBLISHER_VERSION: v1.8.6
    # SHA-256 of mcp-publisher_linux_amd64.tar.gz in that release (line 5 of its checksums file). Update both together.
    MCP_PUBLISHER_SHA256: 1fbe93fc0783c2394d8012c8d6e50a59e98cb2cc2d216264cc69f405d0e21340
and replace lines 67-69 with
  archive="${RUNNER_TEMP}/mcp-publisher_linux_amd64.tar.gz"
  curl -fsSL -o "${archive}" "https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/registry/releases/download/${MCP_PUBLISHER_VERSION}/mcp-publisher_linux_amd64.tar.gz"
  echo "${MCP_PUBLISHER_SHA256}  ${archive}" | sha256sum -c -
  tar xzf "${archive}" -C "${RUNNER_TEMP}" mcp-publisher
  "${RUNNER_TEMP}/mcp-publisher" login github-oidc
  "${RUNNER_TEMP}/mcp-publisher" publish
In docs/publishing.md:64, after 'download mcp-publisher', add: 'and check it against that release's checksums file: shasum -a 256 -c --ignore-missing registry_<version>_checksums.txt'. I tested that command on macOS. The checksums file comes from the same release, so it catches corruption, not a full swap; `cosign verify-blob` with the .sigstore.json bundle is stronger. findings.fix_assessment:
The reviewer's logic is right. Against the stub, it opened one issue, then edited it and commented on later runs. It opened a fresh issue only after the old one was closed. GitHub's search finds quoted title phrases that contain "/" and "-" (tested with a GET to search/issues on cli/cli).

There are two problems:
1. `| head -n1` hides a failed `gh issue list`. GitHub's default shell is `bash -e {0}`, without pipefail (github/docs data/reusables/actions/supported-shells.md:4-5). With a stub whose lookup fails, the reviewer's step exited 0 and opened duplicate #2. Picking the first match inside jq, with no pipe, makes the step fail instead: exit 1, no new issue. gh's own jq handles `[...][0].number // empty`; I tested this with gh api on a GET.
2. Lag in the search index could still let two runs a few minutes apart both create an issue. I didn't check this; it's unlikely.

Not tested: `gh issue list --search` itself, because it sends a GraphQL POST.

findings.title: Dispatch inputs are pasted straight into the shell script, and the API key is exposed to the CLI install
findings.summary: evals.yml:32 pastes `${{ inputs.runs }}` and `${{ inputs.max_cost_usd }}` into the script text, in a step whose environment holds ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. The `npm install -g` on line 30 also runs with that key set. In an emulation of GitHub's substitution, a crafted value ran its own command and dropped `--max-cost-usd`, and an ordinary "$5" reached the CLI as an empty ceiling. Only users with write access can start this workflow, and today that is only the owner.

claims.claim: The inputs are expanded into the script text before bash runs it, in a step whose environment holds ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.
claims.evidence: evals.yml:27-28 set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY for the whole step. evals.yml:32: `--runs "${{ inputs.runs }}" --max-cost-usd "${{ inputs.max_cost_usd }}"`. GitHub's script-injections.md:46: the expressions "are evaluated and then substituted with the resulting values, which can make it vulnerable to shell command injection."

claims.claim: A value such as `1" ; <command> ; echo "` runs arbitrary commands.
claims.evidence: In the emulation, the injected command wrote its marker file. The rest of the line, including `--max-cost-usd 5`, went into `echo`, so claude ran without the ceiling flag.

claims.claim: The inputs have no type, so typos pass unchecked.
claims.evidence: evals.yml:8-13 give only a description and a default. Some values change silently: a cost typed as "$10" reaches the CLI as "0", and "$5" as "", because bash expands $1 and $5 inside the double quotes. The plugin-eval docs (line 369) say the flag's default is "No ceiling". How the CLI treats an empty value is not checkable here.

claims.claim: Only users with write access can start the workflow, and GitHub notes they can already read the repository's secrets.
claims.evidence: data/reusables/repositories/permissions-statement-write.md, used by manually-run-a-workflow.md: "Write access to the repository is required to perform these steps." secure-use.md:33: "Any user with write access to your repository has read access to all secrets configured in your repository." Collaborators today: vipul-goel (admin) only. 0 secrets are configured.

claims.claim: The key is in the environment of `npm install -g`, whose postinstall (`node install.cjs`) doesn't need it.
claims.evidence: `npm view @anthropic-ai/claude-code@2.1.312 scripts` shows postinstall "node install.cjs". I read install.cjs without running it: it copies the platform's native binary over bin/claude.exe and reads no ANTHROPIC variable. @anthropic-ai/claude-code-linux-x64@2.1.312 has no lifecycle scripts. The same vendor's binary gets the key on the next line, so this part is hygiene rather than a real exposure.

I tried the exploit angle. Starting the workflow needs write access, write users can already read secrets, and only the owner has access. So the injection gives nobody anything new today. That limits the severity, not the defect.

I checked whether the double quotes protect the values. They don't stop a `"` or a `$` (emulated).

I checked for a fix after 34d9caa: nothing under .github changed.

The install-time exposure is real but small, because the binary installed by the same packages receives the key next.

audit.reasoning:
evals.yml:32 pastes `${{ inputs.runs }}` and `${{ inputs.max_cost_usd }}` into the script text. evals.yml:27-28 put ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in that step's environment, which includes the `npm install -g` on :30. The practical defect is accidental. A cost typed as "$5" reaches the CLI as an empty string, because bash expands $5. I read the pinned 2.1.312 binary's code without running it: `maxCostUsd:e.maxCostUsd?parseFloat(e.maxCostUsd):void 0`. An empty string counts as false, so the run gets no ceiling and the non-negative check is skipped. "$10" becomes "0", a ceiling of 0, so nothing starts and the run exits 2 (plugin-evals.md:402).

The key reaching the install is hygiene only. The package has no dependencies, and install.cjs reads no ANTHROPIC variable.

Nothing changed since 34d9caa. Minor.

- Read evals.yml:1-40.

The flag is parsed as `maxCostUsd:e.maxCostUsd?parseFloat(e.maxCostUsd):void 0`. The non-negative check is `if(n.maxCostUsd!==void 0&&(...))`. Runs is parsed as `runs:e.runs?Fu(e.runs):void 0`, and the help text says its default is "case.runs ?? 3". No case.yaml sets runs. The installed 2.1.317 has the same cost-flag logic.

- Claude Code docs (curl code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-evals.md): :369 gives "No ceiling" as the default, :383 says to pin both models, :402 gives exit 2.
- GitHub docs (github/docs 7fa55a0): script-injections.md:46; secure-use.md:33 and :67-69; manually-run-a-workflow.md:26-28; workflow-syntax.md:332-338.
- Ruby's YAML parser on the reviewer's one-line env gave Psych::SyntaxError. The verifier's fixed file, rebuilt from its proposed_fix, parses. With the env approach, crafted values reach the CLI literally, but a blank cost still reaches it as `--max-cost-usd ""`.
- GET requests: collaborators are vipul-goel (admin) only, and the repository has 0 Actions secrets.
audit.evidence_errors: "How the CLI treats an empty value is not checkable here" is wrong. It can be read from the pinned binary without running it. The code parses the cost only when the value is truthy and validates it only when it is defined, so "" means no ceiling. The same holds in the installed 2.1.317. That the option parser passes "" through as the value is my reading of the code; I didn't run it.
audit.fix_corrections:
The verifier's fix works as far as it goes. It parses, and crafted values and "$5" reach the CLI literally; "$5" then fails the CLI's own number check.

But a blank input still reaches the CLI as `--max-cost-usd ""` (tested), and the pinned CLI reads that as no ceiling. A blank runs value falls back to 3 runs per case and arm. A blank can come from `gh workflow run -f max_cost_usd=` or from a field the user cleared. Whether `type: number` or `required: true` stops a blank on GitHub's side is not checkable here.

So add `required: true` to both inputs, and make these the first lines of the run step:
  case "$RUNS" in ''|*[!0-9]*) echo "::error::runs must be a whole number"; exit 1;; esac
  case "$MAX_COST_USD" in ''|*[!0-9.]*) echo "::error::max_cost_usd must be a number such as 5"; exit 1;; esac
Keep the messages fixed; don't echo the raw input into a `::error::` line.

Tested with the stubs: "5" and "2.5" run. A blank, "$5" and a crafted runs value stop with exit 1, and nothing else runs. File: <scratch>/work/audit-workflows-other/sim30/evals-corrected.yml (Ruby parses it).

findings.fix_assessment:
The reviewer's direction is right, and it matches GitHub's advice to use an intermediate environment variable (secure-use.md:67-69). Tested in a copy: with the inputs passed through env and quoted, the crafted value and "$5" reach the CLI as literal arguments, nothing else runs, and the install step no longer sees the key.

One error: the reviewer's one-line `env: { ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: ${{ ... }}, RUNS: ..., MAX_COST_USD: ... }` is not valid YAML. Ruby's parser raises a SyntaxError, because `{` and `}` end plain values inside a flow mapping. Write the env as a block mapping.

Not checked: whether `type: number` makes GitHub reject non-numbers when the workflow is started, and how the CLI treats "", "0" or "$5". Running claude plugin eval is off-limits here.

Outside this finding: the CI section of the plugin-eval docs (line 383) also advises pinning both models, and evals.yml doesn't.
findings.proposed_fix:
In .github/pending-workflows/evals.yml (.github/workflows/ after step 2):

1. Inputs (lines 8-13): add `type: number` to both, with numeric defaults:
      max_cost_usd:
        description: Hard cost ceiling for the run, in USD
        type: number
        default: 5
      runs:
        description: Runs per case and arm
        type: number
        default: 1

2. Replace the "Run the eval suite" step (lines 26-33) with two steps. Write the env as a block mapping:
      - name: Install Claude Code
        run: npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code@2.1.312
      - name: Run the eval suite
        env:

          RUNS: ${{ inputs.runs }}
          MAX_COST_USD: ${{ inputs.max_cost_usd }}
        run: |
          claude plugin eval . --trust-plugin --no-publish \
            --runs "$RUNS" --max-cost-usd "$MAX_COST_USD" \
            --allow-tools Write Edit --scaffold -j 3 --json eval-results.json

findings.area: GitHub workflows (.github/pending-workflows: ci, release, evals, verify-data)
findings.title: GitHub switches the monthly check off after 60 quiet days, the same span after which entries count as stale
findings.summary: GitHub's docs say scheduled workflows in a public repository are switched off after 60 days without repository activity, and this repository is public. Entries go stale after the same 60 days. So when the re-verification commit is the last activity, the switch-off comes before the first run that would see stale entries, and the reminder never opens. docs/publishing.md:96-101 doesn't mention this.

claims.claim: In a public repository, GitHub disables scheduled workflows after 60 days with no repository activity.
claims.evidence: github/docs main (7fa55a0, 2026-11-02), events-that-trigger-workflows.md:967 and data/reusables/actions/scheduled-workflows-disabled.md: "In a public repository, scheduled workflows are automatically disabled when no repository activity has occurred in 60 days." `gh api repos/vipul-goel/prompt-engine` shows visibility public.

claims.claim: Entries count as stale after 60 days, so a quiet repository loses the reminder just when it's needed.
claims.evidence: verify-data.yml:27 uses `Date.now() - 60 * 864e5`. Say the entries were verified, and last committed, on 2026-10-29. They are stale from 2026-12-28, the workflow is switched off after 2026-12-28, and the first stale run (2027-01-03) never happens. If the last activity is later, for example a merge on 2026-11-10, the 2027-01-03 run comes first and opens the issue.

claims.claim: Nothing says so, and publishing.md:98 promises an issue once a month.
claims.evidence: docs/publishing.md:98: "opens an issue once a month when an entry ... hasn't been checked for 60 days". A git grep for inactiv, turned off, disabled and "60 days" in docs, README, CONTRIBUTING, CHANGELOG and .github finds no note about the switch-off.

claims.claim: What GitHub counts as repository activity, and whether it warns anyone before switching a workflow off.
claims.evidence: The GitHub pages I read neither define activity nor describe a warning. A web search found nothing either. Whether GitHub e-mails the owner is unverified.

An active repository never hits this, because any activity within 60 days keeps the workflow on. But the reminder is only needed in quiet spells, so the claim stands.

audit.reasoning:
GitHub's docs say scheduled workflows in a public repository are switched off after 60 days without repository activity (events-that-trigger-workflows.md:967 and data/reusables/actions/scheduled-workflows-disabled.md). This repository is public. verify-data.yml:27 uses the same 60 days for staleness.

So when the re-verification commit is the last activity, the switch-off almost always comes before the first run that sees stale entries. Over two years of verification dates and four commit times, the issue never opened in 2,876 of 2,924 cases. It opens only when the 60th day falls on the 3rd and the commit came after 06:17 UTC. Any later activity, such as merging the PR, moves the switch-off and lets the issue open.

publishing.md:96-101 promises a monthly issue and says nothing about the switch-off.

A switched-off workflow can't just be run by hand. gh's `workflow run` offers only active workflows, and `gh workflow enable` lists the ones switched off for inactivity.

Confidence is medium. GitHub doesn't define "activity", and one 2026 user report says schedules kept running 70 to 120+ days after the last commit. The missing doc note is a defect either way; changing the schedule or window is the owner's call.

With the 60-day window, 2,876 of 2,924 cases never open an issue. A monthly cron needs a window of at most 29 days (30 days misses 28 cases). A weekly cron needs at most 53 (54 misses 208).

findings.fix_assessment:
A doc note is the right minimum, but two parts of the reviewer's text are off.
- "Or run it by hand" doesn't work on its own. GitHub's troubleshooting page says "A disabled workflow does not respond to its triggers" (troubleshoot-workflows.md:74), so the workflow has to be re-enabled first.
- "If the issue stops appearing" asks the maintainer to notice a missing issue they had no reason to expect.

A structural fix needs the stale window to end before the switch-off by more than the gap between runs: at most 29 days with the monthly cron, at most 53 with a weekly one. That changes the monthly, 60-day design in plan.md:193. Without the fix for 29, it would also multiply the duplicates. So it is the owner's call.
findings.proposed_fix:
Add to docs/publishing.md under "Monthly data check", after line 98: "GitHub turns off scheduled workflows in a public repository after 60 days without repository activity, and a turned-off workflow doesn't respond to its triggers. Entries go stale after the same 60 days, so in a quiet repository the issue may never open. When you come back after a quiet spell, open Actions → Re-verify tool data. If it's turned off, click Enable workflow, then Run workflow."

Only if the owner wants the check to fire before the switch-off: run it weekly (for example cron '17 6 * * 1') with a 45-day window. That means changing verify-data.yml:3-4, :7, :27 and :38 and publishing.md:98 together. Do it only with the fix for 29 in place; even then, each weekly run adds a comment unless that comment is dropped.

findings.area: GitHub workflows (.github/pending-workflows: ci, release, evals, verify-data)
findings.title: Any v* tag publishes without CI's checks and without confirming the commit is on main
findings.summary: On this branch, pushing the tag v<plugin version> runs release.yml from the tagged commit, merged or not. It publishes the GitHub release, npm (once NPM_TOKEN is set) and the MCP Registry, and npm and the registry never accept a version twice. It runs validate.mjs and the Node 22 MCP tests but skips the script tests, `claude plugin validate`, Node 20 and the Inspector gates, and nothing checks that the commit is on main or passed CI, although publishing.md:52 requires a merge first. release.mjs stops tags that don't match the version, and the workflows are parked, so the gap is latent until step 2.

claims.claim: The release job runs validate.mjs (through release.mjs) and the MCP tests on Node 22 only.
claims.evidence: release.yml:18-27: node-version 22, then npm ci, build and test. release.yml:28-29 call release.mjs, and release.mjs:30 runs validate.mjs, which also checks generated files (validate.mjs:215-217).

claims.claim: It skips `claude plugin validate . --strict`, the scripts/test suite, the Node 20 run and the Inspector gates.
claims.evidence: ci.yml has them: :24-25 script tests, :28-31 plugin validate, :39 node [20, 22], :51-53 test:inspector. release.yml has none of them. mcp/package.json:35-37 declares engines node >=20.

claims.claim: Nothing enforces publishing.md:52 ('Merge to main, then tag the merge commit').
claims.evidence: Neither release.yml nor release.mjs checks it. GET rulesets returns []. main returns 404 'Branch not protected'. The repo has no environments.

claims.claim: Any v* tag, including one on an unmerged or unreviewed commit, goes to npm and the registry.
claims.evidence: github/docs events-that-trigger-workflows.md (push): GITHUB_SHA is the 'Tip commit pushed to the ref', and push 'includes workflows that are not merged into the default branch'. But release.mjs:24-28 stops any tag that isn't v<plugin version> at that commit: v9.9.9 and v0.1.0-rc.1 both exit 1 in my copy. So 'any v* tag' is overstated. A tag on the version-bump branch head does publish.

claims.claim: Neither npm nor the registry lets you publish that version number again.
claims.evidence: npm/cli v12.2.1 docs npm-publish.md:59: 'that specific name and version combination can never be used again, even if it is removed with npm unpublish'. The registry rejects duplicates (v1.8.6 registry_service.go:279-280). A publisher can still mark a registry version deprecated or deleted (v1.8.7 handlers/v0/status.go:24, :82-84).

claims.claim: Fix: a compare status of `identical` or `behind` for main...SHA means the commit is on main.
claims.evidence: Tested today: compare/main...4ba0a01 (main) gives identical 0 0; compare/main...3956d22 (the pushed branch) gives ahead 31 0; compare/3956d22...main gives behind 0 31.

claims.claim: Fix: calling ci.yml as a local reusable workflow with `needs: ci` runs CI on the tagged commit.
claims.evidence: github/docs data/reusables/actions/reusable-workflow-calling-syntax.md: with a `./` reference, 'the called workflow is from the same commit as the caller workflow'. reusing-workflow-configurations.md:91: token permissions 'can be only downgraded (not elevated) by the called workflow'.

findings.refutation: Fixed after 34d9caa? No: release.yml and ci.yml are unchanged since 7fb1b1a. 'Any v* tag' is overstated, because release.mjs:24-28 stops tags that don't match the version. The realistic mistake remains: tagging the version-bump branch head. CLAUDE.md step 5 uses Squash and merge, so that head never lands on main. 'Without CI's checks' is partly overstated: validate.mjs, including the generated-file check, and the Node 22 tests do run. Only accounts with write access can push tags, which today means the owner. So this guards against mistakes, not attackers; someone with push access could also tag a commit whose release.yml lacks the check. An on-main check doesn't prove review either, because main has no protection. plan.md records no decision on release gating, and publishing.md:52 already states the policy the check would enforce, so I record this as confirmed (minor), with an owner question on how to gate.

audit.reasoning: The facts hold, but whether this is a defect depends on release policy. Facts I re-checked: release.yml runs on any v* tag push (:5-7). It uses Node 22 only (:20). It runs the MCP tests (:22-27) and release.mjs (:28-29), which runs validate.mjs (release.mjs:30), including the stale generated-file check (validate.mjs:215-217). It skips the script tests (ci.yml:24-25), `claude plugin validate` (ci.yml:28-31), Node 20 (ci.yml:39) and the Inspector gates (ci.yml:51-53). Nothing checks that the commit is on main: there are no rulesets, main is unprotected, and there are no environments. Two parts of the finding are overstated. 'Any v* tag' is wrong: release.mjs:24-28 stops any tag that isn't v<plugin version>. In my copy, v9.9.9, v0.1.0-rc.1 and v0.1 each exited 1 and wrote no dist/. 'Without CI's checks' is partly wrong: validate and the Node 22 tests do run. The script tests and `claude plugin validate` check the validator and the plugin, and the plugin ships from main, not from a release. Also, publishing.md:37-51 has the maintainer run the full list of checks before tagging, which the verifier didn't cite. What's left is a guard against mistakes. vipul-goel is the only collaborator, and CLAUDE.md step 5 and plan.md:188 have Claude ask before pushing any tag. plan.md records no decision on release gating. It did plan for release tooling to boot the packed server on Node 20 and 22 (plan.md:134), which nothing does today. Each remedy has a cost. An on-main check rules out a hotfix release from a branch. Re-running CI adds minutes and more ways for a release to be blocked: a flaky test, or a failed claude-code npm install. And 'on main' proves nothing about review while main is unprotected. Those are the owner's choices.
